parts.title: Watching an Elephant's Ear Temperature Automatically: Using Infrared Cameras and Deep Learning to Monitor Asian Elephants
parts.abstract:
Simple Summary

Asian elephants have a hard time getting rid of body heat. They are huge, so they have little skin surface compared with the amount of body inside. They also have almost no sweat glands, the tiny structures that let many animals cool down by sweating. Measuring an elephant's internal body temperature is an important way to check how hot or cold it is inside. The usual ways of doing this, though, need people to get close to the animal, need the animal to cooperate, and mean handling it by hand again and again.

In this study, we asked whether we could use infrared thermal images together with deep learning, a kind of artificial intelligence that learns from examples, to track the temperature of an elephant's ear automatically. An infrared thermal camera makes pictures in which each spot shows how warm it is. We studied eight Asian elephants living in a semi-captive setting, meaning they live in an enclosure but are not fully confined. At the same time, we measured the temperature of the skin surface, the temperature inside the body (using a thermometer placed in the rectum), and the conditions of the surroundings.

Of all the body parts we looked at, the outer ear was the one most closely linked to the internal temperature. We then trained and compared eight lightweight object-detection models, which are small, fast computer programs that learn to find a particular object in a picture. We used 2372 infrared images for this. All of the models found the outer ear well. One of them, called YOLO11n, gave the best overall balance between how well it picked out the right temperature and how fast it worked.

Our approach lets people check the temperature of the ear surface quickly, without touching or disturbing the animal, and again and again. If it is tested further under different weather and health conditions, it may help with routine checks on the welfare of elephants in human care and with spotting unusual temperatures early. It may also help with monitoring the bodies of wild elephants from a distance.

Keywords: Asian elephant, infrared thermography (infrared temperature imaging), auricular temperature (ear temperature), thermal window (a body area that lets heat escape), animal welfare, deep learning, YOLO, non-invasive monitoring (monitoring without touching or disturbing the animal)
parts.introduction_first:
The Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) is a large mammal that keeps its body temperature steady, much as we do. To stay in balance, it has to keep adjusting how much heat it takes in and gives off, both through its behavior and through its body's own processes. But it has only a small amount of skin surface compared with its huge body, very little hair, and almost no sweat glands. This limits how well it can lose heat through its skin, and it raises concerns about whether it can cope as the temperature around it changes [1].

Asian elephants live mostly in tropical and subtropical regions, where the air can be as warm as the elephant's body or even warmer. As the climate changes, many of the places where they originally lived are expected to become warmer and drier [2], and extreme heat and cold may happen more often. These changes may threaten both the survival of wild Asian elephants and the welfare of elephants that people care for.
parts.conclusion:
5. Conclusions

In this study, we built and tested a deep-learning system that works without touching or disturbing the animal. It automatically finds the outer ear in infrared pictures of Asian elephants and reads off the temperature of the ear surface. What is new at its heart is that we first checked, using earlier knowledge of how an elephant's body works, which body area is useful for tracking temperature, and then built the automatic detection system around that choice.

We compared three body areas. Of these, the outer ear showed the strongest positive link with rectal temperature, meaning that when the ear was warmer, the internal temperature tended to be warmer too. This supports the ear as a body area that tells us something useful about temperature without disturbing the animal. Still, this link is only moderate in strength. So ear temperature cannot stand in directly for the temperature inside the body, and it should be read as a sign of temperature at the outer edge of the body.

All eight lightweight YOLO models were good at finding the outer ear. We found an important lesson about how to choose a model for measuring temperature. The usual scores for how well a model finds an object are not enough on their own. A model's box can sit slightly off-center, and that small shift can change the temperature values it gives, especially the highest temperature. YOLO11n gave the most balanced overall performance, combining how accurately it found the ear, how closely its temperatures matched the hand-measured ones, and how fast it worked. We chose it as the preferred model for real-world use.

Our system offers a fast, non-invasive way to check ear surface temperature in a standard way for Asian elephants in human care, and it needs little computing power. Right now, its main use is to measure temperature at the outer edge of the body automatically. It is not meant to predict the temperature inside the body directly or to diagnose fever or heat stress. Testing it further on more elephants and in more kinds of weather and conditions will help it be used for a wider range of purposes.
parts.introduction_rest:
To understand how well Asian elephants can cope with heat, we first need a reliable way to measure their internal body temperature. Earlier research found that Asian elephants have an average internal temperature of about 36.1 °C, with recorded values from 35.9 to 37.1 °C. Their internal temperature changed only a little as the temperature around them changed [3]. The usual way to estimate an elephant's internal temperature is to place a thermometer in the rectum and read it by hand. For this, the animal has to be trained to cooperate while it is awake. The person also has to get close to the animal and handle it again and again. This makes the method unsuitable for collecting large amounts of data taken often.

For this reason, people have become more and more interested in automatic ways of tracking internal body temperature. These include tiny chips and sensors placed inside the body [4,5], and temperature sensors placed on the outside of the body or inside it [6]. Several small temperature recorders, which are waterproof and do not corrode, have been used to measure the internal temperature of Asian and African elephants at set times [7]. Kinahan and colleagues trained African savanna elephants living in captivity to swallow small temperature recorders called iButtons. The recorders passed through the gut, and the team collected them afterwards. In this way they recorded the daily rise and fall of the elephants' internal temperature [8].

Weissenböck and colleagues built reusable capsules that recorded the temperature inside the gut and sent the readings wirelessly, in both Asian and African elephants [3]. Their results showed that the internal temperature of Asian elephants followed a daily rhythm. It was highest around midday and lowest in the early morning, roughly matching the daily changes in the temperature around them. Still, sensors given by mouth have practical problems. Chewing can damage them, nobody knows how long they take to pass through the gut, and they are lost when the animal poops. So we need a more efficient way to check how hot or cold an elephant is inside, one that disturbs the animal less.

The temperature of the skin surface tells us a lot about how an elephant loses heat and controls its body temperature [9]. Unlike the internal temperature, though, the surface is directly exposed to the surroundings, and it differs a lot from one body area to another. A reading from a single spot may therefore not show the temperature of the whole animal.

Infrared temperature imaging is a way to see these patterns of surface temperature without touching or disturbing the animal. It has been used more and more to check how the bodies of mammals are working [10]. It has several advantages. It can be run from a distance, it collects data quickly, it disturbs the animal very little, and it can show how temperature is spread over fairly large parts of the body. Because of this, it has been used in studies of animal bodies and of animals in the wild. These studies have used it to spot disease, to follow breeding, to study behavior, and to judge how hot or cold an animal is [11,12].

How accurate infrared temperature imaging is, however, depends on the surroundings, on the animal itself, and on the equipment. The surroundings include direct sunlight, rain, wind, the temperature of the air, and how humid the air is. The equipment matters too: how far the camera is from the animal, and the angle or field of view. The animal's own features can also affect how well changes in temperature are measured. These include how thick the hair is, what color it is, the condition of the coat, how thick the skin is, and how wet the surface is [11,12]. Large mammals with little hair and mostly bare skin, such as elephants and rhinoceroses, are therefore especially good subjects for infrared temperature imaging [13].

Infrared temperature imaging has already been used to study how elephants' bodies work in their natural surroundings and how they control their body temperature. Earlier studies have all shown that the outer ear is a major thermal window, a body area that lets heat escape. This is because the ear has a large network of blood vessels and a large surface that is open to the air. Its temperature changes clearly when the elephant is active or when it is cold [14,15,16]. Infrared temperature imaging has also proved useful in veterinary care, because it can catch inflammation of the ear early: a small patch of the ear becomes warmer before any visible signs appear [17]. Overall, the outer ear is a key place for Asian elephants to adjust their body temperature, and it could be useful for checking their health early.

Infrared temperature imaging is well suited to measuring the temperature of the outer ear in Asian elephants. But there is a problem. To get a temperature value, someone has to choose the area of interest on each picture and read the temperature by hand. This takes a long time and delays real-time monitoring [18]. Computer methods based on artificial intelligence have therefore become more and more important for monitoring animals automatically. Deep-learning object-detection models can find animals or body areas accurately, even when the background is busy or the object is partly hidden. This means people do not have to process the pictures by hand again and again [19].

The You Only Look Once (YOLO) family of models finds objects in a single pass through the picture, so they work very fast. Improved versions of YOLO have been shown to recognize objects reliably even in busy scenes, which makes them well suited to real-time use [20,21]. Because of this, YOLO models are now widely used in wildlife studies to find animals, sort them into groups, and keep track of individual animals.

When combined with infrared temperature imaging, deep-learning systems have been built mainly for poultry and farm animals, including pigs, dairy cows, and sheep [22,23,24,25]. These systems fall into three broad types. The first finds body areas and then reads the temperature directly from them [26]. The second marks each pixel of the picture, which gives a more precise temperature for each area [27]. The third uses machine-learning models to estimate the internal temperature, or how hot or cold the animal is, from the pattern of temperatures on the surface [28,29,30].

It is important to note that finding the right area is not enough on its own to show that an automatic temperature system works. The temperatures it gives must also be carefully checked against temperatures measured by hand [24,26]. Just as important is choosing the right body area in advance. The chosen area must be shown to be linked to the internal temperature, rather than picked only because it is easy to work with [31].

Taken together, these studies show that it is technically possible to combine body areas that make sense for temperature with computer vision, so that we can check how an animal's body is working without touching or disturbing it. Even so, two important gaps in knowledge remain. First, most automatic infrared studies pick body areas directly, without first checking in a careful, step-by-step way how those areas are linked to the internal temperature. This risks that the temperature being tracked means little about the animal's body. Second, no such automatic temperature system has been built for Asian elephants. This species has its own special limits on how it controls body temperature. Its outer ear is central to heat exchange in the body, and it is also easy for a computer to find, because of its distinct shape and the strong difference in temperature between it and its surroundings.

To fill these gaps, we set out to do four things. (1) We compared how rectal temperature was linked to the surface temperature of three body areas: the head, the outer ear, and the body and legs together. This let us find the area that tells us the most for automatic monitoring. (2) We trained and compared eight lightweight YOLO models to find the chosen area automatically in infrared pictures. (3) We took the average and highest temperatures from the area each model found, by matching the model's box to the original temperature grid of the picture. (4) We judged and ranked the models by how well they found the area, how fast they worked, and how closely their temperatures matched the hand-measured ones.

We designed this system to give a fast way to check the temperature of the outer ear in Asian elephants without touching or disturbing the animal. It could be used for routine checks on welfare, for keeping watch on how hot or cold elephants are, and, in the future, for monitoring wild elephants from a distance. Our work also makes four key new contributions. First, it is the first study to compare three possible body areas for temperature in Asian elephants in a careful, step-by-step way. It uses a method called repeated-measures correlation, which takes into account that we measured the same elephants again and again. Second, it builds the first deep-learning system that automatically finds the outer ear and reads its temperature in infrared pictures of Asian elephants, testing eight lightweight YOLO designs from four generations. Third, it offers a way to choose a model using several measures at once: the usual scores for finding an object, how well the temperatures match, and practical points about using the system in real life. It checks how reliable this choice is with a Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis, which means running the analysis many times with slightly different settings to see how much the result changes. Fourth, it shows that the very small YOLO11n model strikes a good balance between how accurately it reads temperatures and how fast it works. This makes it a possible candidate for running on small, portable computers at the scene, for real-time temperature monitoring without touching or disturbing the animal in places where elephants are cared for.
parts.results:
3. Results

3.1. Choosing the Best Body Area to Track Temperature

We first wanted to know which body area's temperature was most closely linked to the temperature inside the body. For each body area, we compared its temperature with the rectal temperature, the thermometer reading from inside the body. We used a method called repeated-measures correlation. It measures how closely two things rise and fall together, but it is built for cases where the same animals are measured again and again over time.

Every body area and every condition of the surroundings we tested showed a statistically significant link with rectal temperature (df = 417, all p < 0.001). "Statistically significant" means that if there were really no link, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. Here, p < 0.001 means less than 0.1% of the time.

We looked at three body areas: the head, the outer ear, and the trunk and legs together. For each one, we used two kinds of measurement. The first was the average temperature across the area. The second was the highest temperature found anywhere in the area. Table 2 lists all of them.

Among the averages, the outer ear came out on top. Its average temperature was most closely linked to rectal temperature, with a correlation of 0.395. The head came next at 0.392, and the trunk and legs at 0.381. The highest temperatures were linked a little more weakly. The outer ear's highest temperature reached 0.362, the head's 0.331, and the trunk and legs' 0.307.

Table 2

How closely the temperature of each body area and each condition of the surroundings was linked to the rectal temperature of Asian elephants.

| | rrm | dof | p | 95% CI

| AT | 0.305 | 417 | <0.001 | [0.22, 0.39]

| RH | −0.241 | 417 | <0.001 | [−0.33, −0.15]

| HTavg | 0.362 | 417 | <0.001 | [0.27, 0.45]

| ETavg | 0.395 | 417 | <0.001 | [0.3, 0.48]

| T&LTavg | 0.331 | 417 | <0.001 | [0.24, 0.42]

| HTmax | 0.392 | 417 | <0.001 | [0.3, 0.48]

| ETmax | 0.307 | 417 | <0.001 | [0.21, 0.4]

| T&LTmax | 0.381 | 417 | <0.001 | [0.29, 0.47]

AT, air temperature; RH, relative humidity (how much moisture is in the air); HTavg, average head temperature; ETavg, average outer-ear temperature; T&LTavg, average trunk-and-leg temperature; HTmax, highest head temperature; ETmax, highest outer-ear temperature; T&LTmax, highest trunk-and-leg temperature. The rrm column gives the repeated-measures correlation. The 95% CI column gives the 95% confidence interval, a range of values that fit our data well.

Before we started, we had set a rule for choosing a body area. Following that rule, we picked the average outer-ear temperature as the measurement to use in the rest of our work. This is the measurement our automatic system would find and read off.

3.2. Finding the Outer Ear Automatically

Figure 2 shows typical results from our eight trained models: YOLOv5n, YOLOv5s, YOLOv8n, YOLOv8s, YOLO11n, YOLO11s, YOLO26n, and YOLO26s. All eight models found the outer ear in the infrared pictures, which were 256 × 192 pixels in size. They did not all do it in exactly the same way, though. They differed in how confident they were and in where they placed their box around the ear.

Figure 2

Typical results from eight YOLO models (YOLOv5n, YOLOv5s, YOLOv8n, YOLOv8s, YOLO11n, YOLO11s, YOLO26n, and YOLO26s) finding the outer ear of an Asian elephant. Each box marks the outer ear the model found, and the number next to it is the model's confidence score.

Table 3 shows how well each model found the ear on its own, using a separate set of pictures that we had held back for testing. We used three scores. Precision tells us how often a model's box really held the ear. Recall tells us how many of the real ears the model managed to find. The F1 score combines the two into one number.

All the models did a satisfactory job on both counts. YOLOv8s did best overall. Its precision was 92.9%, its recall was 92.4%, and its F1 score was 92.6%. YOLOv8n and YOLO11n also did well. YOLOv5n had the lowest precision and F1 score of all the models.

Table 3

How well each of the eight YOLO models found the outer ear.

| Model | Training Images | Validation Images | Precision (%) | Recall (%) | F1 (%) | mAP50 | FPS

| YOLOv5n | 1974 | 204 | 85.5 | 89.8 | 87.6 | 0.923 | 213

| YOLOv5s | 90.2 | 90.4 | 90.3 | 90.4 | 92.6 | 0.92 | 108

| YOLOv8n | 91.9 | 91.8 | 91.8 | 91.8 | 91.8 | 0.936 | 133

| YOLOv8s | 92.9 | 92.4 | 92.6 | 92.4 | 92.6 | 0.94 | 99

| YOLO11n | 91.8 | 90.9 | 91.3 | 90.9 | 91.3 | 0.933 | 164

| YOLO11s | 90.0 | 91.3 | 90.6 | 91.3 | 90.6 | 0.929 | 110

| YOLO26n | 90.8 | 90.3 | 90.5 | 90.3 | 90.5 | 0.936 | 189

| YOLO26s | 89.8 | 91.4 | 90.6 | 91.4 | 90.6 | 0.947 | 53

We also used a score called mAP50. It measures how well a model finds the object overall, and a value of 1 would be perfect. All eight models scored at least 0.920, which shows that they generally found the outer ear well. YOLO26s scored highest, at 0.947, followed by YOLOv8s at 0.940. YOLOv5s scored lowest, at 0.920.

In most of the YOLO families, the larger "s" models scored slightly higher than the matching "n" models. This suggests that a bigger model has a small advantage in accuracy. Speed showed the opposite pattern. The lighter "n" models worked faster than the matching "s" models. YOLOv5n was the fastest, handling 213 frames per second (FPS). YOLO26n came next at 189 FPS, then YOLO11n at 164 FPS. Among the "s" models, YOLOv5s, YOLO11s, and YOLOv8s worked at similar speeds of 108, 110, and 99 FPS. YOLO26s was the slowest, at 53 FPS. So the "n" models were clearly more efficient to run. They may therefore be better suited to live, real-time use or to devices with limited computing power.

3.3. Reading Off Ear Temperature Automatically and Checking How Well It Matches

The scores above told us how well each model found the outer ear and placed its box. But they did not tell us whether the box was in a good enough place to give a reliable ear temperature. So we combined the trained models with the original infrared pictures, which store a temperature for every pixel. This let us read off the temperature inside each box the model had drawn. We did this on a separate set of pictures that we had kept aside for testing.

To compare against, we used temperatures measured by hand. We drew the ear area by hand using Fluke Connect software, a program for infrared cameras, and then read off its temperature. We should be clear about what these hand measurements mean. They were our reference for drawing the ear area and reading its temperature. They are not the true, exact temperature of the ear tissue. Even trained people can draw the edge of the ear slightly differently each time. Also, an infrared camera measures the temperature of the surface from the heat it gives off. It does not measure the temperature deep inside the tissue. That reading also depends on the camera's emissivity setting, which describes how well a surface gives off heat. It is affected by sunlight and other light from the surroundings that bounces off the surface. So the comparisons below show how well the automatic and hand methods agree with each other. They do not show how close the temperatures are to some imagined true temperature.

For each model, we looked at two temperature values. The first was the average temperature of all the pixels inside the box. The second was the highest temperature inside the box. We compared the automatic and hand values in two ways. The first was a Bland–Altman analysis. It shows how far apart the two sets of values are, and whether the gap changes as the temperature gets higher. The second was a Taylor diagram, which we describe in Section 3.3.3.

3.3.1. How Well Average Ear Temperature Matched

Figure 3 shows the Bland–Altman plots comparing the average outer-ear temperatures from the automatic and hand methods for the eight YOLO models.

Figure 3

Bland–Altman plots comparing average outer-ear temperatures measured by hand and by the eight YOLO models. (a) YOLOv5s; (b) YOLOv5n; (c) YOLOv8s; (d) YOLOv8n; (e) YOLO11s; (f) YOLO11n; (g) YOLO26s; (h) YOLO26n. The solid horizontal line shows the average difference, or bias, between the automatic and hand values. The dashed horizontal lines show the 95% limits of agreement, the range in which most of the differences fall.

For every model, the average bias was smaller than 0.15 °C, whether the model read too high or too low. This means the models did not keep reading the average ear temperature much higher or lower than the hand values. YOLOv5n had the smallest bias, at −0.02 °C, followed by YOLO26n at −0.04 °C.

The models differed more in how wide their 95% limits of agreement were. A narrower range means the automatic and hand values agreed more closely. YOLO26s had the narrowest range, from −0.641 to 0.489 °C, a total width of about 1.13 °C. This showed that YOLO26s gave the most consistent average temperatures of all eight models. YOLOv5s and YOLO11s also had fairly narrow ranges. For YOLOv5s, the range ran from −0.707 to 0.503 °C. For YOLO11s, it ran from −0.721 to 0.548 °C. The full Bland–Altman results are in Table S2.

3.3.2. How Well the Highest Ear Temperature Matched

Figure 4 shows the Bland–Altman plots comparing the highest outer-ear temperatures from the automatic and hand methods.

Figure 4

Bland–Altman plots comparing the highest outer-ear temperatures measured by hand and by the eight YOLO models. (a) YOLOv5s; (b) YOLOv5n; (c) YOLOv8s; (d) YOLOv8n; (e) YOLO11s; (f) YOLO11n; (g) YOLO26s; (h) YOLO26n. The solid horizontal line shows the average difference, or bias, between the automatic and hand values. The dashed horizontal lines show the 95% limits of agreement.

In general, the bias and the limits of agreement were larger for the highest temperature than for the average temperature. YOLOv8s had the smallest bias for the highest temperature, at −0.125 °C. YOLO26s had a bias of −0.227 °C, and YOLOv8n had a bias of −0.295 °C.

The models differed most in the width of their 95% limits of agreement. YOLOv8s had the narrowest range, from −1.138 to 0.889 °C, a total width of about 2.03 °C. This showed that YOLOv8s gave the closest match between automatic and hand readings of the highest outer-ear temperature.

By contrast, YOLOv5n and YOLO11s had much wider ranges. For YOLOv5n, the range ran from −5.535 to 6.069 °C, a width of about 11.60 °C. For YOLO11s, it ran from −6.190 to 6.736 °C, a width of about 12.93 °C. These wide ranges showed that these two models gave very variable readings of the highest temperature. The full Bland–Altman results are in Table S2.

In several of the YOLO families, the "s" model had a narrower range than the matching "n" model. This suggests that, in some families, the larger models may have given steadier temperature readings. But the link between model size and how well it read temperatures was not the same for every model design.

3.3.3. Comparing All the Models on One Chart

A Taylor diagram brings three measures together into a single chart, so we can compare the automatic and hand temperatures side by side (Figure 5). The first measure is the correlation coefficient, which shows how closely the two sets of values rise and fall together. The second is the standard deviation, which shows how spread out the values are. The third is the centered root-mean-square difference, which shows the typical size of the gap between the automatic and hand values.

Figure 5

Taylor diagrams comparing outer-ear temperatures measured by hand and by the automatic models. (a) Average outer-ear temperature; (b) highest outer-ear temperature. The blue circle marks the hand-measured values. Models closer to the blue circle agree more closely with the hand values.

For the average temperature, every model sat close to the blue circle, which shows that all of them agreed well with the hand values. YOLO11n did best overall. Its correlation coefficient was 0.9986, its standard-deviation ratio was 1.014, and its typical gap (RMSD) was 0.262 °C. YOLO26n came a close second, with a correlation coefficient of 0.9986, a standard-deviation ratio of 1.022, and an RMSD of 0.282 °C.

For the highest temperature, the models were more spread out. YOLOv8s sat closest to the blue circle, with a correlation coefficient of 0.984, a standard-deviation ratio of 1.009, and an RMSD of 0.565 °C. According to the values in our original analysis, YOLOv5s sat farthest from the blue circle. It had a correlation coefficient of 0.942, a standard-deviation ratio of 1.079, and an RMSD of 1.115 °C. The full Taylor diagram results are in Table S3.

Overall, the Taylor diagram results broadly agreed with the Bland–Altman results. Together, the two methods pointed to YOLOv8s and YOLO11n as the leading models for reading off ear temperature automatically. However, which model came out ahead was different for the average and the highest temperature.

3.4. Ranking the Models by Combining Several Measures

We followed the two-stage plan for choosing a model that we described in Section 2.6.3. First, we gave each model a combined score for reading off the average temperature and a separate combined score for reading off the highest temperature. Then we looked at how steady each model was across both tasks and how fast it worked, to pick the final best model.

For each model, we combined seven measures into one score. These were the detection rate, the size of the bias, the standard-deviation ratio, the correlation coefficient, the centered RMSD, the F1 score, and the mAP50. Before combining them, we put all seven on the same scale so that no single measure would count for more just because of its units. Table 4 shows the final rankings and scores.

Table 4

Rankings of the eight YOLO models for reading off average and highest temperatures, with their combined scores.

| Rank | Mean-Temperature Model | Composite Score | Maximum-Temperature Model | Composite Score

| 1 | YOLO11n | 0.727 | YOLOv8n | 0.861

| 2 | YOLOv8n | 0.628 | YOLO26n | 0.815

| 3 | YOLO26s | 0.445 | YOLO11n | 0.776

| 4 | YOLOv8s | 0.431 | YOLOv8s | 0.770

| 5 | YOLO26n | 0.428 | YOLO11s | 0.663

| 6 | YOLO11s | 0.400 | YOLO26s | 0.633

| 7 | YOLOv5n | 0.278 | YOLOv5n | 0.556

| 8 | YOLOv5s | 0.196 | YOLOv5s | 0.157

For the average temperature, YOLO11n had the highest combined score, at 0.727. YOLOv8n came second with 0.628, followed by YOLO26s with 0.445. YOLOv5s had the lowest score, at 0.196.

For the highest temperature, YOLOv8n had the highest combined score, at 0.861. YOLO26n came second with 0.815, followed by YOLO11n with 0.776. YOLOv5s again came last, with 0.157.

So YOLOv5s came last for both the average and the highest temperature. This shows that it did comparatively poorly at reading off ear temperature automatically. YOLOv5n also came near the bottom in both rankings.

YOLO11n was the steadiest model across the two tasks. It came first for the average temperature and third for the highest temperature. YOLOv8n was also consistent, coming second for the average and first for the highest temperature.

We also wanted to check whether our choice depended on the weights we gave each of the seven measures. To do this, we used a Monte Carlo approach, which means repeating a calculation many times with random changes. We changed each weight by a random amount of up to 20% above or below its starting value. We did this 1000 times, each time rescaling the weights so they added up to the same total, and then ranked the models again.

Table S4 shows the results. For the average temperature, YOLO11n came first in all 1000 of the 1000 repeats, and YOLOv8n came second every time. For the highest temperature, YOLOv8n came first in all 1000 repeats, while YOLO11n came within the top three in 64.6% of them.

It is worth noting that the lightweight "n" models usually ranked higher than the matching "s" models in this combined ranking. This goes against the usual expectation that larger models always perform better. It shows that how well a model reads off temperatures does not depend only on how well it finds the ear. Placing the box in the same spot each time may matter especially when the temperature is read directly from the pixels inside the box.

We weighed the rankings for both average and highest temperature, along with how fast each model works and what might be needed for real-world use. Taking all of this into account, we chose YOLO11n as the preferred model for reading off outer-ear temperature automatically. It came first for the average temperature, with a combined score of 0.727, and third for the highest temperature, with a combined score of 0.776. It performed strongly on both temperature measures. It also worked fast, at 164 FPS, much faster than YOLOv8s at 99 FPS and YOLO26s at 53 FPS. We therefore chose YOLO11n for building the rest of the system and for possible real-time use.
parts.discussion:
4. Discussion

4.1. Why the Outer Ear Matters for Controlling Body Temperature in Asian Elephants

Of the three body areas we studied, the outer ear was the one most closely linked to rectal temperature, our measure of the temperature inside the body. On average, the two rose and fell together in a moderate way. This supports using the outer ear as a useful place to track changes in an Asian elephant's temperature without touching or disturbing the animal. It does not mean that ear temperature is the same as the temperature inside the body, or that it can replace that measurement directly without first checking how well it predicts it.

Some body areas act as "thermal windows": special places on the surface that let heat pass between an animal and its surroundings. These areas usually have many blood vessels close to the surface, fairly little insulation, and the ability to adjust how much blood flows through them. Some studies define a thermal window as a small patch of skin whose temperature differs from the skin right next to it by more than about 5 °C [34]. The elephant's outer ear is especially well suited to this job. It has a lot of surface compared with its volume, very little hair, and a large network of blood vessels. When an elephant flaps its ears, the inner surface of the ear is again and again exposed to moving air. This helps the ear lose heat in two ways: through the air flowing across it, and through heat given off as radiation. In this way, blood flowing through the vessels near the ear surface can carry heat from inside the body out into the surroundings [35].

Earlier studies using infrared thermal cameras have given consistent evidence for this role. Weissenböck and colleagues studied six African elephants kept outdoors at temperatures from −4.1 to 7.5 °C and indoors at 15.0 to 20.3 °C. They found thermal windows in 43.9% of their measurements, and the size, shape and temperature of the ear windows varied a great deal [36]. Lefebvre and colleagues studied how 10 Asian elephants controlled their body temperature in cold winter conditions. They found thermal windows mainly on the ears, and whether they appeared, and where, was linked to the age of each elephant. Under the cold conditions they studied, however, they found no statistically significant link between the temperature of the surroundings and whether thermal windows appeared [37]. Studies of physical activity have also shown the ear's role in controlling temperature. Rowe and colleagues showed that Asian elephants build up a lot of body heat during exercise that is not at their hardest, and that they rely on their behavior to cope with the limits their large bodies place on cooling down [15]. Tilley and colleagues later reported clear changes in surface temperature across different body areas in active Asian elephants, with the ears showing especially important temperature responses [16].

Our results add to these observations. They show that outer-ear temperature stays linked to rectal temperature even under the fairly mild resting conditions of our study. This suggests that the ear works not only as a place for actively getting rid of heat during exercise or in extreme weather, but also as a body area that may be useful for routine temperature checks. Still, the link between ear temperature and rectal temperature is moderate, not strong enough to estimate the temperature inside the body directly. So outer-ear temperature should be seen as a sign of temperature at the outer edge of the body. How it relates to the temperature inside the body depends on how the blood vessels are controlled, the conditions around the animal, its behavior, and the features of each individual elephant.

4.2. Why the Models Performed Differently

The eight YOLO models were generally very good at finding the outer ear. Within several of the model families, the larger "s" versions scored slightly higher than the matching "n" versions on a common accuracy score called mAP50. This score measures how well a model finds the right object, counting a box as correct when it overlaps the real object by at least half. For example, YOLOv8s scored 0.940, compared with 0.936 for YOLOv8n. This broadly fits the idea that models with more internal settings to learn may be better at placing their boxes.

However, when we ranked the models by how well they picked out the right temperature, the order was different. YOLO11n came first for the average temperature, while YOLOv8n came second. For the highest temperature, YOLOv8n came first and YOLO11n came third. So, in this overall comparison that weighed several things, the lighter "n" models generally did better than the matching "s" models.

This shows that a model's usual accuracy at finding an object does not necessarily match how well it picks out the right temperature. A model's box can be good enough to count as correct on the mAP score, yet still include or leave out pixels (the tiny dots that make up a picture) that change the temperature it reads. This matters most for the highest temperature, because that value may depend on just one or a few very hot pixels.

Earlier studies that measured animal temperature automatically have also shown that it is important to check both how well a model finds the body part and how well it reads the temperature from that part [24,25,26]. Xie and colleagues combined deep learning for finding body parts with temperature reading in pigs. They showed that how useful the model was in practice depended on both how well it placed its boxes and how well it measured temperature [24]. Zhang and colleagues also checked how closely automatic readings of sheep eye temperature matched hand measurements [26].

One possible reason for the results we saw is that some lighter models placed their boxes more consistently, even though their usual mAP scores were slightly lower. A more complex model, on the other hand, could in theory shift its box by a little. Such a small shift might barely change the mAP50 score but could change which temperature pixels are included. This idea is still only a hypothesis. It should be tested by directly measuring how far the boxes are shifted, how big they are, and how much they overlap the outer ear area that we marked by hand.

In the end, we chose YOLO11n because it performed fairly steadily for both the average and the highest temperature, while still working very fast, at 164 frames per second. It therefore gave a good balance between finding the ear, matching the hand-measured temperatures, and using little computing power. However, this model should not be seen as better than the others in every case, because its ranking depended partly on how we weighted the different things we measured in our overall comparison.

4.3. Limits of Our Methods

Several limits of our methods should be kept in mind when reading our findings.

First, both the hand-marked areas and the boxes found by YOLO were rectangles. Using the same shape for both meant that the automatic and hand measurements were compared over areas of the same kind. But a rectangle cannot follow the uneven outline of an elephant's ear exactly. So some boxes may have included nearby parts of the head or body, or the background. This may matter most for the highest temperature, because a few pixels outside the ear that are unusually hot could greatly change the value we read. Methods that mark the exact outline of each body part, pixel by pixel, may therefore outline the ear more accurately. Shu and colleagues, for example, used an improved version of a deep-learning design called U-Net to outline the warm areas on the faces of dairy cows and to read the temperature of each area automatically [25]. Future studies could test YOLO models that outline objects, or other designs of this kind, to outline the elephant's outer ear precisely.

Second, the surface temperature measured by an infrared camera depends on many things: the temperature of the surroundings, how humid the air is, wind speed, direct sunlight, moisture on the surface, how far the camera is, the angle it looks from, the emissivity of the surface (how well it gives off heat as infrared light), and heat reflected from the background [12,27]. We took our pictures in the shade and tried to avoid body surfaces that looked wet, but we did not correct the temperatures for these effects after reading them. A recent study of rabbits built a machine-learning model that corrected infrared temperatures using measurements of the surroundings [38].

We measured the conditions of the surroundings 10 cm above the ground. This captures the air close to the ground that resting elephants experience, but it does not fully match the air at the height of the ear. This mismatch may limit how accurate any later correction of surface temperatures would be. For distance, we took all infrared pictures from the same distance of 5 m. This matches standard veterinary practice for infrared imaging, and it makes sure that the small spot the camera measures is small enough compared with the ear to measure the ear's temperature reliably. However, because we always used this fixed distance, we have not checked how well the model picks out the right temperature when pictures are taken from farther away, as is typical when monitoring wild elephants.

We set the emissivity to 0.98, the value commonly used for human skin. We did not independently check whether this value suits Asian elephant skin. Future studies could strengthen their temperature readings by calibrating for each species, using contact temperature measurements or a reference blackbody (a standard object that gives off a known amount of heat).

Third, we used a Bland–Altman analysis to compare the temperatures read automatically with those read by hand from the same infrared pictures. This method checks how closely two sets of readings agree. The small differences we saw for the average temperature therefore show that the two ways of choosing the ear area agree well. They do not show that the infrared camera measured the true temperature of the elephant's ear with an error below 0.15 °C. The camera we used, the Fluke TiS55+, is stated to be accurate to within ±2 °C under the conditions it is designed to work in. So how well the automatic and hand readings agree should be kept separate from how accurate the camera's temperature readings are. In the same way, agreement between automatic and hand readings of the ear does not show that either one estimates rectal temperature or the temperature inside the body equally accurately.

Finally, we used a type of analysis called repeated-measures correlation to study the link between ear temperature and rectal temperature. This kind of analysis takes into account that repeated measurements from the same elephant are not independent of each other. However, our correlation models did not statistically account for conditions of the surroundings. We collected our body measurements from eight semi-captive elephants kept at one study site. Although we collected 425 measurements taken at matching times, differences between individual elephants in age, sex, body weight, control of blood flow, skin condition, behavior and health may still affect the link between ear temperature and rectal temperature. Future analyses could add the temperature of the surroundings, humidity and time of day to mixed-effects models, a type of analysis that can separate the effects of different factors, to better isolate the link between the temperature inside the body and at the outer edge without the surroundings muddying it. Before the links we found could be applied to the species as a whole, they would also need to be checked on elephants from other institutions or populations.

4.4. Predicting the Temperature Inside the Body in the Future

In this study, we successfully built an automatic method for finding the outer ear and reading its surface temperature. However, we did not build a reliable enough model for predicting rectal temperature or the temperature inside the body from outer-ear temperature.

Future studies should record a fuller set of conditions of the surroundings, including the temperature of the surroundings, humidity, wind speed, sunlight, and possibly rain or how wet the surface is. These could be added to models that predict from several factors at once, either through multiple regression (a statistical method that estimates how several factors together relate to an outcome) or through machine learning.

Machine-learning methods have already been used to estimate the temperature inside the body, or how hot an animal is, from infrared surface measurements. Joy and colleagues combined infrared temperatures of different body areas with machine learning to assess heat stress and estimate rectal temperature in sheep [28]. Yuan and colleagues compared several prediction models for estimating the temperature inside the body of female rabbits from infrared pictures [29]. Pacheco and colleagues used deep learning to sort dairy cows into different temperature conditions based on infrared images [30]. These studies show that predictions of temperature generally work better when surface temperature is combined with information about the surroundings and the animal's body.

For Asian elephants, future prediction models could include: the highest and average outer-ear temperature; how temperature is spread across the ear; the temperature of the surroundings and humidity; wind speed and sunlight; time of day; which elephant it is; age, sex and body weight; recent physical activity; ear-flapping behavior; and health or signs of inflammation.

Possible ways to build such models include mixed-effects regression, random forests, extreme gradient boosting and deep neural networks. These are different machine-learning methods, some of which combine many simple decision rules and others that learn in layers. When building the models, we should test them on data held back from training, using data from different elephants each time, and also test them on elephants that were not part of the training. This will help avoid making the models seem better at predicting than they really are.

4.5. Possible Uses in Caring for and Protecting Elephants

The automatic method we built for reading ear temperature can be used directly in the routine care of Asian elephants in human care, both in full captivity and in semi-captive settings. The lightweight YOLO11n model works at 164 frames per second, so it can handle infrared pictures from fixed monitoring cameras as they are taken. This makes it possible to check the ear surface temperature often and without touching or disturbing the animal, without the heavy work of processing pictures by hand.

Checking the temperature automatically again and again can help animal care staff spot when an elephant's temperature moves away from its usual pattern. Such changes may point to changes in how much heat the surroundings are putting on the animal, in how active it is, or in how blood is flowing to the outer parts of its body. Because the model is lightweight, it could also run on a small computer at the site itself, in places with little computing equipment or poor internet connection, where processing pictures on site is better. This way of using a lightweight model, with the work done on the device itself, fits the idea of "augmented intelligence of things": instead of sending every task to a central computer, the work is spread to small local devices. This reduces the need for a constant internet connection and helps field monitoring systems respond faster. This approach has been shown to work securely and efficiently in small, low-resource internet-connected devices, which supports using our temperature monitoring method in this way [39].

We must stress that the system is not yet checked as a tool for diagnosing fever, infection or heat stress, and the temperature levels that should trigger a warning still need to be set. Using it to monitor wild elephants from a distance, for example from drones, is a longer-term research goal. That would need much more testing, because the distance to the animal changes, plants can block the view, and the animal is not held still.

Overall, the main immediate value of the system is that it measures the ear surface temperature automatically and in a standard way from infrared pictures. This gives a foundation for future studies of how temperature works in the body, and for monitoring the welfare of Asian elephants in human care.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Where and Whom We Studied

We carried out this study from August 2025 to June 2026 at the Wild Elephant Valley Scenic Area. It is in Mengyang Town, Jinghong City, in the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture of Yunnan Province, China (22°10′ N, 100°51′ E), 795 m above sea level. The animals were Asian elephants kept at the Yunnan Asian Elephant Rescue and Breeding Center. We studied eight elephants living in a semi-captive setting: five females and three males. They were between 3 and about 40 years old (Table S1). All of them were used to regular contact with the people who care for them.

2.2. How We Collected the Data

2.2.1. The Equipment We Used

We measured four things: the temperature inside the body, the temperature of the skin surface, the temperature of the air, and the relative humidity (how much moisture is in the air). For each one we used a different device. A small temperature logger called the iButton DS1922L (Maxim Integrated Products, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA) recorded the internal temperature. A Fluke TiS55+ infrared thermal camera (Fluke Corporation, Everett, WA, USA) took infrared pictures of the body surface. A BENETECH GM1365 logger (Shenzhen Benetech Instrument Co., Ltd., Shenzhen, Guangdong, China) recorded the air temperature and humidity.

The iButton logger could measure from −40 to 85 °C. It was accurate to within ±0.5 °C between −10 and 65 °C, the range in which it had been calibrated, meaning checked against known temperatures. The BENETECH logger measured from −30 to 80 °C and was accurate to within ±0.3 °C between 10 and 60 °C. It measured relative humidity from 0 to 100%, accurate to within ±2%. The Fluke camera could measure from −20 to 550 °C, although it had not been calibrated below −10 °C. Its stated temperature accuracy was ±2 °C when the air was 25 °C. The camera took infrared and ordinary color pictures at the same time, and its infrared detector had a resolution of 256 × 192 pixels.

2.2.2. How We Collected the Data

We used rectal temperature as a stand-in for the temperature inside the body. When an elephant we were watching had a bowel movement, we gently placed a lubricated iButton logger into its rectum, about 30 cm in. The logger was about 17.3 mm across and 6 mm thick, and we coated it with petroleum jelly. We set it to record the temperature every 5 minutes. The next time the elephant had a bowel movement, usually 1 to 3 hours later, the logger came out with the droppings. We then collected it, cleaned and disinfected it, and connected it to its software to download the readings.

Once we had started measuring rectal temperature, we also recorded the air temperature, the relative humidity and the skin-surface temperature at the same 5-minute intervals. The air temperature and humidity came from the BENETECH logger, which we placed on a stand about 10 cm above the ground in the elephant enclosure, in a spot shielded from direct sunlight. We took the infrared pictures of one side of each elephant with the Fluke camera from about 5 m away. We set the camera's "reflected background temperature" to the measured air temperature. We also set its emissivity to 0.98. Emissivity describes how well a surface gives off infrared heat, and 0.98 is a value widely used in infrared studies of elephants and other large, sparsely haired animals [14].

During the fieldwork, we measured the eight elephants again and again. This gave us 425 sets of measurements taken at the same moment: rectal temperature, skin-surface temperature, air temperature and relative humidity, each paired with one infrared picture. We knew for certain which elephant each of these 425 pictures showed. To give our models more examples to learn from, we also added older infrared pictures that our research group had taken at the same site. These were taken between March 2016 and January 2020, and between November 2023 and October 2024, and they show Asian elephants in semi-captive, captive and wild settings.

All the pictures, old and new, were taken with the same camera hardware, resolution, calibration steps, emissivity settings, distances and standard procedures. The people taking them had been trained in the same way within our research group. The older pictures did not record which elephant was shown, so we cannot say exactly how many different elephants appear in the full set of 2372 pictures. However, we checked that none of the eight semi-captive elephants from our new measurements appeared in the older pictures.

We first checked all the older pictures and then picked some of them at random to build the final, larger set. We left a picture out if it met any of these rules, which we had decided on in advance: (1) it was badly blurred by movement or out of focus; (2) the camera was looking at the elephant from more than 45° away from the side; (3) the camera was more than 4.5 m or less than 5.5 m away; or (4) more than half of the outer ear was hidden by plants, other elephants or parts of the enclosure. After this check, we picked the remaining older pictures at random in a balanced way, so that captive, semi-captive and wild elephants, and different field seasons, were fairly represented. In total, we kept 2372 infrared pictures (425 new and 1947 older) for building the dataset.

2.3. Choosing Which Body Area to Find Automatically

Using Fluke Connect software (version 2.0.10.0), we divided each elephant's body surface into three body areas: the head, the outer ear, and the body and legs (Figure 1). The software then read off the skin-surface temperature of each area directly.

Figure 1

Example of the body areas marked on an infrared picture of an Asian elephant: (A) head; (B) outer ear; and (C) body and legs.

Whether a person draws the area by hand or a computer finds it, the measurement can be off if the chosen area includes some pixels of the background. We saw that the elephants' skin stayed warmer than the background in every season. So, for each area, we described its surface temperature using both the highest temperature and the average temperature inside the area.

We measured the same eight elephants many times, so their repeated readings were not independent of each other. A simple correlation, such as the usual Pearson or Spearman correlation, would treat each reading as if it came from a different animal, which is a mistake called pseudoreplication. To avoid this, we used a method called repeated-measures correlation (rmcorr). It removes each elephant's own starting level, so that repeated readings from the same animal do not count as extra evidence. We then looked for a straight-line link between the skin-surface temperature of each area and the rectal temperature. The body area with the strongest link, whether positive or negative, was chosen in advance as the one the computer would find.

2.4. Building the Dataset

We marked the outer ear by hand on every infrared picture using the LabelImg image annotation tool (version 1.8.6). One trained person did all the marking, so that differences between people's judgments would not creep in. We drew a box around the outer ear using the same body landmarks every time. The box covered the whole ear, from the tip at the top to the base at the bottom, and from where the ear joins the head inwards to the outer edge of the ear. We saved all the boxes in YOLO format, so we could later train the models and check how well they found the ear.

We split the full set of 2372 marked pictures into three groups, in a ratio of about 9 to 1 to 1: 1974 pictures for training, 204 for validation and 194 for an outside test. The validation pictures are used to check a model while it learns, and the outside test pictures are kept aside for a final check. Both groups came only from the 425 new pictures from this study. We split them by elephant, so that no elephant appeared in both groups. The training pictures were the rest of the new pictures plus all the older ones. Importantly, every picture in the outside test set came from a different Asian elephant that did not appear in either the training or the validation set. This gave us a strictly independent test of how well the models measured temperature.

2.5. Finding the Outer Ear Automatically and Reading Its Temperature

2.5.1. Choosing the YOLO Models and Their Sizes

We combined infrared pictures with deep learning so that a computer could find the outer ear automatically and read off its surface temperature.

The You Only Look Once (YOLO) family of object-detection methods is built on deep convolutional neural networks, a type of deep learning that is especially good at spotting patterns in pictures. YOLO finds objects in a single pass through the whole picture, from start to finish, and can do this in real time [32,33]. Instead of searching step by step, it predicts directly where each object's box is and how likely the object is to belong to each class. This lets it find and name objects quickly and accurately, with little delay, and the designs can be scaled up or down [33].

YOLO models usually come in five sizes: nano (n), small (s), medium (m), large (l) and extra-large (x). The smaller ones, especially n and s, usually work faster and need less computing power. The larger ones may find objects more accurately but need more computing power. A system for watching wildlife automatically may in the end need to run on a small computer placed close to the camera. Running it there means fewer large pictures need to be sent to distant online computers, the delay is shorter, the data are more private, and it may be especially useful in remote places with poor internet.

We wanted a balance between accuracy, speed and the chance of running on a small computer with limited power. So we chose four generations of YOLO: YOLOv5, YOLOv8, YOLO11 and YOLO26. For each generation, we tested the two lightest sizes, n and s. This gave us eight models: YOLOv5n, YOLOv5s, YOLOv8n, YOLOv8s, YOLO11n, YOLO11s, YOLO26n and YOLO26s. We trained and tested all eight at the same time. We wanted to see how well each one found the outer ear in the infrared pictures, and to find the model best suited to measuring ear temperature automatically and possibly in real time.

2.5.2. How We Trained the Models

We wanted to be able to repeat our work and to compare all the models fairly. So we trained all eight YOLO models on the same computer, with the same training settings.

We ran every training and testing run on the same computer. It had an AMD Ryzen 9 5900HS processor (Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (AMD), Santa Clara, CA, USA), an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 graphics card with 6 GB of its own memory (NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara, CA, USA), and 16 GB of system memory, running Windows 11. The software included CUDA 11.5, which lets the graphics card do the calculations, Python 3.8.20, and the PyTorch 2.0.1 deep learning toolkit. We built all the models and training steps on the Ultralytics YOLO toolkit.

We kept the main training settings the same for all eight models. Each picture was resized to 640 × 640 pixels. The model looked at 16 pictures at a time, and training could run for at most 80 epochs, where one epoch is one full pass through all the training pictures. To adjust the model step by step, we used a method called stochastic gradient descent (SGD), with a momentum of 0.937 and a weight decay of 0.0005. The learning rate, which controls how big each adjustment is, started at 0.01. We then used a cosine annealing schedule, which lowers the learning rate smoothly over training, with a final learning rate ratio of 0.01.

All models started from settings that had already been learned on COCO, a large, widely used collection of everyday pictures. This is called transfer learning, and it helps the models settle on good settings more reliably. To avoid overfitting, which happens when a model memorizes its training pictures instead of learning general patterns, we used early stopping. Training stopped automatically if the error on the validation pictures had not improved for 15 epochs in a row. We fixed the random starting number (seed = 42) for every run, so that the results could be repeated exactly. After each epoch, we checked the models on the validation set to see whether they were settling down and to trigger early stopping.

During training, we also used data augmentation, which means making small, random changes to the training pictures so the model sees more variety. We flipped pictures left to right, stretched or shifted them, and sometimes stitched four training pictures together into one. We also changed the colors in a way that copies the different color palettes that thermal cameras use to show temperature. We used these changes only for training. When we measured temperature, we used the original, unchanged pictures, so that the measurements stayed accurate.

2.5.3. Reading the Outer-Ear Temperature Automatically

When the Fluke TiS55+ camera took a picture, it also saved a table of temperatures, one value for every pixel in the picture. For each picture, the YOLO model gave the box around the outer ear as four numbers: the left, top, right and bottom positions (x1, y1, x2, y2). We turned these positions into the matching rows and columns of the temperature table. We then took out every pixel's temperature inside the box and worked out the average and the highest temperature of the outer ear.

2.6. Testing the Models and Choosing the Best One

We tested the eight YOLO models in two ways that complement each other. First, we measured how well each one found the outer ear. Second, we checked how closely the temperatures it gave matched the ones we measured by hand. We combined the results of both to choose the model that gave the best balance between finding the ear, matching the temperatures and using little computing power.

2.6.1. How Well Each Model Found the Ear

This part measured how well each model could find and locate the outer ear. We used four scores: precision, recall, F1 score and mean Average Precision (mAP50).

Precision tells us how many of the boxes the model drew were really the ear. Recall tells us how many of the real ears the model managed to find. We calculated them as:

(1) Pr = TP / (TP + FP)

(2) Rc = TP / (TP + FN)

Here, TP (true positives) are boxes that correctly marked the ear, FP (false positives) are boxes that marked something that was not the ear, and FN (false negatives) are real ears that the model missed.

The F1 score combines precision and recall into a single number, using a kind of average called the harmonic mean. It shows how well a model balances the two:

(3) F1 = 2PrRc / (Pr + Rc)

AP (Average Precision) sums up the trade-off between precision and recall for one class of objects, as the area under a curve. mAP (mean Average Precision) is the average of these AP values over all the classes. In this study, we used mAP50. It is the area under the precision–recall curve when a box counts as correct if it overlaps the real ear by at least half (an intersection-over-union of 0.50).

(4) AP = ∫₀¹ P(r) dr

(5) mAP = (1/k) ∑ᵢ₌₁ᵏ APᵢ

We measured speed as frames processed per second (FPS), which shows how suitable each model might be for real-time monitoring.

2.6.2. How Closely the Automatic Temperatures Matched the Hand-Measured Ones

The scores above show how well a model finds the ear, but they do not show whether it reads the right temperature from that area. So we also compared the temperatures from the YOLO boxes with the temperatures from the hand-drawn areas in Fluke Connect software.

We ran each trained YOLO model on the outside test pictures. We recorded the share of test pictures in which the model found the outer ear, which we call the detection rate R. For each picture, we used two temperature values: the average temperature and the highest temperature of all the pixels inside the box. For each model and each of these two values, we checked how well the automatic and hand-measured temperatures agreed, using two tools: Bland–Altman analysis and Taylor diagrams.

Bland–Altman analysis looks at the differences between the two sets of measurements. It gives the average difference, called the bias, and the range in which 95% of the differences fall, called the limits of agreement (LoA = bias ± 1.96 × standard deviation). A bias close to zero and narrow limits of agreement meant that the automatic and hand-measured temperatures agreed more closely.

A Taylor diagram is a single chart that brings several measures together. It used the hand-measured temperature as the reference and showed three things: the correlation coefficient (r), which shows how closely the two sets of values rise and fall together; the standard deviation (σ), which shows how spread out the values are; and the centered root-mean-square difference (RMSD), which shows the typical size of the gap between the two sets. An ideal model would sit close to the reference point, with r = 1, σ = σ_ref and RMSD = 0.

Using both the usual scores for finding objects and a direct check of temperature agreement matters because finding the right body area very accurately does not always mean reading the right temperature [25,27].

2.6.3. Combining Several Scores to Choose a Model

How well a model found the ear and how closely its temperatures matched measured different sides of its performance. So no single score was enough to choose a model. For example, a model with a high mAP50 could still give temperatures that were quite far off on average. On the other hand, a model with a high correlation could miss the outer ear in a large share of pictures, which would make measuring temperature impossible.

We therefore built a way to combine these different sides of performance into one number, called a weighted score. We used seven measures: the detection rate; the absolute temperature bias (the size of the average difference, ignoring whether it is positive or negative); the standard-deviation ratio; the correlation coefficient; the centered RMSD; the F1 score; and mAP50. We gave each measure a weight, a number showing how much it counts toward the total. We based the weights on the main goal of monitoring ear temperature in Asian elephants in practice, on agreement among experts in veterinary infrared thermography, and on common practice in similar studies that watch wildlife automatically. Table 1 lists all the weights.

Table 1

The measures used in the evaluation and how much each one counts (its weight).

| Measure | Weight

| Detection rate | 0.2

| Absolute bias | 0.15

| Standard-deviation ratio | 0.15

| Correlation coefficient | 0.15

| Centered RMSD | 0.15

| F1 score | 0.1

| mAP50 | 0.1

We chose the final model in two steps, following rules we had decided on in advance. First, we worked out a weighted score separately for measuring the average temperature and for measuring the highest temperature, and ranked the models on each. Second, we picked the best model by looking at three things together: (1) how steady the ranking was across both average and highest temperature; (2) how fast the model worked in real time; and (3) how suitable it was for possibly running on a small computer in the field. We had set all of these rules before training and testing the models.

We also wanted to check that our final ranking was not just a result of our own choices about the weights. So we ran a Monte Carlo weight perturbation analysis, a test that nudges the weights at random many times to see how much the answer changes. We changed each of the seven weights at random by up to 20% above or below its starting value, and did this 1000 times to get 1000 different sets of weights. Each time, we rescaled the weights so that they still added up to the same total, which kept the scores on the same scale. For every set of weights, we worked out each model's weighted score and rank again.

The seven measures were on different scales, and for some of them a higher number was better while for others a lower number was better. So we rescaled every measure to run from 0 to 1, with higher numbers always meaning better performance.

For measures where higher is better, such as the detection rate (R) and the correlation coefficient (r), we calculated the rescaled score as:

(6) Sᵢ = (Xᵢ − Xmin) / (Xmax − Xmin)

For measures where lower is better, such as the absolute bias and the RMSD, we calculated it as:

(7) Sᵢ = 1 − (Xᵢ − Xmin) / (Xmax − Xmin)

For the standard-deviation ratio, the best value was 1, so we calculated it as:

(8) Sᵢ = 1 − |σratio,ᵢ − 1| / maxⱼ(|σratio,ᵢ − 1|)

Here, Xᵢ is the original value of the measure for model i, and Xmin and Xmax are the smallest and largest values among the eight models.

We calculated the overall weighted score as:

(9) Stotal = 0.2Sdet + 0.15Sbias + 0.15Scorr + 0.15Sstd + 0.15SRMSD + 0.1SF1 + 0.1SmAP50

Here, Sdet, Sbias, Scorr, Sstd, SRMSD, SF1 and SmAP50 are the rescaled scores for the detection rate, absolute bias, correlation coefficient, standard-deviation ratio, centered RMSD, F1 score and mAP50.

We ranked the eight models from the highest overall score to the lowest. The model with the highest score was chosen as the preferred model for finding the outer ear automatically and measuring its temperature.
